_README: Destinations content. Place names & facts are real; descriptions are editorial. Any hard number (visitor stats) comes from data/facts.json via factId. No invented hours/prices/distances.

myeongdong.name: Myeongdong
myeongdong.blurb: Shopping, street food and beauty — the classic first stop.
intro: Myeongdong is Seoul's busiest shopping street and the most-visited area for foreign travelers. It's packed with cosmetics shops, fashion, and a lively evening street-food scene.
It's central and easy to reach, which makes it a natural base or first stop on day one.

Beyond the shops, the landmark Myeongdong Cathedral rises just above the district, and the streets are a hub for K-beauty flagships and duty-free stores. After dark the main lanes turn into one of Seoul's best street-food scenes — tteokbokki, hotteok and grilled skewers.
tips: Come hungry in the evening — the street-food carts are the highlight.
Beauty shops often give free samples; compare a few before buying.
Line 4 Myeongdong Station, exits 5–8, drop you in the middle of it.
Bring your passport — many stores offer tax-free or duty-free shopping for visitors — and consider an evening show at the nearby Nanta theater.

gyeongbokgung.name: Gyeongbokgung Palace
gyeongbokgung.blurb: Grand royal palace — wear a hanbok for free entry.
intro: Gyeongbokgung is the largest of Seoul's Joseon-era royal palaces, with grand gates, courtyards and a scenic pavilion over a pond.
Renting a hanbok (traditional dress) nearby lets you enter free and makes for memorable photos.

First built in 1395 as the main palace of the Joseon dynasty, Gyeongbokgung centres on the Geunjeongjeon throne hall, and its grounds hold the National Palace Museum and the National Folk Museum — enough to fill a half-day if you explore in full.
tips: Wear a hanbok for free palace entry.
Try to catch the changing-of-the-guard ceremony at the main gate.
Bukchon Hanok Village is a short walk away — pair them in one morning.
The palace is closed on Tuesdays; free English-guided tours run daily, and arriving at opening time beats both the crowds and the midday heat.

n-seoul-tower.name: N Seoul Tower
n-seoul-tower.blurb: Namsan cable car and the city's best skyline.
intro: Perched atop Namsan mountain, N Seoul Tower gives the best panoramic view over the city, especially at sunset and after dark.
The Namsan cable car up the hill is part of the fun.

First opened in 1980 as a broadcast tower, N Seoul Tower crowns Namsan mountain, so its observation deck looks out over the whole city and the Han River. The railings and walls below are famous for thousands of couples' 'love locks'.
tips: Go near sunset to catch both day and night views.
Take the cable car up; you can walk down through Namsan Park.
Weekends and holidays get busy — arrive early or late.
Ride the cable car or hike up Namsan (buses also reach the base). The observatory and restaurants stay open late, making it an easy evening stop after Myeongdong.

bukchon.name: Bukchon Hanok Village
bukchon.blurb: Traditional hanok lanes and photogenic viewpoints.
intro: Bukchon is a hillside neighborhood of preserved hanok (traditional houses) between two palaces, with quiet lanes and rooftop views.
It's a living residential area, so it rewards a calm, respectful stroll.

Set on the hill between Gyeongbokgung and Changdeokgung palaces, this centuries-old quarter is famous for its 'Bukchon Hanok 8 Views' photo spots, and many of its old houses now hold craft workshops, tea houses and tiny museums you can step into.
tips: Keep your voice down — people live here.
Mornings are quietest for photos.
Combine with Gyeongbokgung and Insadong nearby.

The classic viewpoints are up the steep Gahoe-dong lanes; signs ask visitors to keep quiet during residents' morning and evening hours, and a free area map is available at the neighborhood info center.

hongdae.name: Hongdae
hongdae.blurb: Street performances, indie shops and nightlife.
intro: Hongdae, around Hongik University, is Seoul's youthful arts-and-music district — buskers, indie boutiques, clubs and late-night eats.
It's the place to feel the city's energy after dark.

The district grew up around Hongik University, Korea's top art school, which shaped its indie-music and street-art character. Weekends fill the 'Hongdae playground' with buskers and free live shows, and the old railway is now the leafy Gyeongui Line Forest Park, nicknamed 'Yeontral Park'.
tips: Evenings bring out the street performers.
Explore the side streets for cafes and vintage shops.
Well connected by Line 2 and the AREX airport line.
It sits on the AREX line linking both Incheon and Gimpo airports, so it's a favourite first or last night in Seoul; nightlife peaks Friday and Saturday and runs very late.

seongsu.name: Seongsu
seongsu.blurb: A converted-factory district of design cafés and ever-changing K-pop and brand pop-up stores.
intro: Once an industrial area, Seongsu is now Seoul's coolest café and design district — converted warehouses, specialty roasteries and concept stores.
It's also where K-pop agencies and brands run a constant stream of pop-up stores, idol-themed cafés and photo events, which is why fans treat it as a must-visit.

Nicknamed 'Seoul's Brooklyn', the area was once a hub of shoe factories and metal workshops. From the mid-2010s its raw brick-and-concrete spaces were reborn as galleries, flagship stores and rooftop cafes, and SM Entertainment's headquarters and its KWANGYA@SEOUL store now anchor its constant K-pop pop-ups.
tips: Cafe-hop — many roasters and dessert spots sit within a few blocks.
Check for current K-pop or brand pop-ups before you go (SM Entertainment's KWANGYA@SEOUL store is here too); they change often and some need a timed reservation.
Pair it with Seoul Forest park next door, and come on a weekday for calmer streets.
Pop-ups and idol cafes rotate weekly, so check what's on and whether a slot needs booking; the district is easy to walk and pairs with Seoul Forest and the riverside just south.

bukhansan.name: Bukhansan (K-Hiking)
bukhansan.blurb: Granite peaks on the city's edge — Korea's fastest-growing trend.
intro: Bukhansan National Park rises right at Seoul's edge, with granite peaks and temple trails — and it leads the surging 'K-hiking' trend among foreign visitors.
Trails range from easy walks to steep scrambles, so pick one to match your fitness.

The park's highest point, Baegundae, tops out at 836 m in a granite scramble with fixed chains and sweeping city views. Its slopes are wrapped by the old Bukhansanseong fortress walls and dotted with temples like Doseonsa, and it ranks among the world's busiest national parks.
tips: Start early in the morning, especially in summer.
Wear proper shoes; upper sections are rocky.
Check the weather and carry water.
Ride the subway to a trailhead such as Bukhansan Ui or Gupabal, wear grippy shoes for the smooth granite near the top, and skip the exposed ridges in rain or ice.

dmz.name: DMZ Tour
dmz.blurb: The border zone — visited on an organized tour.
intro: The Demilitarized Zone between South and North Korea is a striking day trip from Seoul, usually done via an organized tour that handles access and rules.
Stops can include observatories and infiltration tunnels.

Created by the 1953 Armistice, the DMZ is a strip about 4 km wide running roughly 250 km across the peninsula. Tours typically take in Imjingak park, the Third Infiltration Tunnel and the Dora Observatory looking into the North; decades sealed off have made it an unexpected haven for wildlife.
tips: You must join an authorized tour — you can't go independently.
Bring your passport; there are ID checks.
Book ahead, especially in peak season.

Tours to the JSA / Panmunjom truce village are separate and stricter (dress code and passport details registered in advance). Access can close at short notice, so book a reputable operator and reconfirm before you travel.

haeundae.name: Haeundae Beach
haeundae.blurb: Busan's most famous beach and seaside district.
intro: Haeundae is Busan's signature beach — a long sandy stretch backed by hotels, cafés and the Blueline Park coastal rail with its colorful sky capsules.
It's the easiest base for a first Busan trip.

The district is more than sand: the Dongbaekseom island trail loops past the Nurimaru APEC House, the SEA LIFE aquarium sits on the beachfront, and Haeundae Traditional Market packs in street food a few blocks back. In summer it's Korea's busiest beach, with festivals and fireworks.
tips: The Blueline Park sky capsule is popular — book ahead in season.
Nearby Gwangalli Beach is best at night for the Diamond Bridge lights.
Seafood restaurants line the back streets.

The Blueline Park beach train runs along the old coastal railway toward Cheongsapo and Songjeong for some of Busan's best sea views — and sunrise over the water is a local ritual worth the early alarm.

gamcheon.name: Gamcheon Culture Village
gamcheon.blurb: Hillside village of brightly painted houses.
intro: Gamcheon is a photogenic hillside neighborhood of pastel houses, murals and art installations, often called Busan's 'Santorini'.
Narrow stepped lanes reward slow wandering.

Built in the 1950s by Korean-War refugees, the stacked hillside houses were transformed from 2009 by an art-village project that added murals, sculptures and galleries through the lanes. The 'Little Prince' statue marks the classic viewpoint over the pastel rooftops.
tips: Wear comfortable shoes — it's hilly with lots of steps.
Follow the art-map stamp trail for the best routes.
It's a residential area, so keep noise down.
Pick up a stamp map at the entrance to find the art spots and hidden cafes; weekday mornings are calmest, and it's a short bus ride uphill from Toseong subway station.

jagalchi.name: Jagalchi Fish Market
intro: Jagalchi is Korea's largest seafood market — pick your catch downstairs and have it prepared upstairs.
It's a lively, authentic slice of Busan's port life.

Rebuilt after the Korean War by the women vendors known as 'Jagalchi ajumma', the market grew into Korea's largest seafood hub and holds a big festival each October. The modern glass building on the waterfront has a rooftop terrace over the harbour.
tips: Go for lunch when it's freshest and busiest.
Prices are often negotiable — agree before you order.
Combine with Gukje Market and BIFF Square next door.

Pick your seafood from the ground-floor tanks, then take it upstairs where a restaurant prepares it (a cooking charge applies) — agree the price first. It sits right beside Gukje Market and BIFF Square.

seongsan.name: Seongsan Ilchulbong
seongsan.blurb: UNESCO sunrise peak on Jeju's east coast.
intro: Seongsan Ilchulbong ('Sunrise Peak') is a dramatic volcanic tuff cone rising from the sea, a UNESCO World Heritage site and Jeju's signature sunrise spot.
The climb to the crater rim is short but steep.

The crater formed about 5,000 years ago from a shallow-sea eruption, leaving a green bowl fringed by jagged peaks — part of Jeju's UNESCO Global Geopark. The surrounding waters are still worked by the island's haenyeo, its women free-divers.
tips: Sunrise is the classic time, but any clear day is stunning.
It's a real climb — wear good shoes.
Pair with Seopjikoji and Manjanggul on an east-Jeju day.
The rim climb is about half an hour up wooden stairs; time it for a haenyeo diving demonstration at the base, and pair it with nearby Seopjikoji and the Manjanggul lava tube.

hallasan.name: Hallasan
hallasan.blurb: Jeju's volcano — trails for every level.
intro: Hallasan is a shield volcano at the center of Jeju and the highest mountain in South Korea, ringed by trails through changing forest and alpine scenery.
Some summit trails require an early start and reservations.

At 1,947 m, Hallasan is South Korea's highest peak — a dormant shield volcano crowned by the Baengnokdam crater lake and ringed by a UNESCO Biosphere Reserve that shifts from broadleaf forest to alpine shrubs, with royal azaleas in spring.
tips: Check which trails reach the summit and whether reservations are needed.
Weather changes fast — bring layers.
Start early to finish within park hours.
Only the Seongpanak and Gwaneumsa trails reach the summit — both long full-day hikes that need an advance reservation. The shorter Yeongsil and Eorimok trails give big views without the summit push.

changdeokgung.name: Changdeokgung Palace
changdeokgung.blurb: UNESCO palace with the famous Secret Garden.
intro: Changdeokgung is the best-preserved of Seoul’s Joseon-era royal palaces and a UNESCO World Heritage site, laid out to follow the natural hillside rather than impose on it.
Its Huwon ‘Secret Garden’, seen on a timed guided walk, is the highlight — especially in autumn.

Built in 1405 as a secondary palace, Changdeokgung became the Joseon kings' favoured residence for much of the dynasty. Its Injeongjeon throne hall and the naturalistic Huwon garden — with lotus ponds and centuries-old trees — earned it the UNESCO World Heritage listing in 1997.
tips: The Secret Garden (Huwon) uses a separate timed ticket — book or arrive early.
Like other palaces it closes one day a week; check hours on the official site.
It pairs naturally with Bukchon and Gyeongbokgung in one morning.
The Secret Garden is entered only on a scheduled guided walk (about 90 minutes) with limited daily places, and the palace closes on Mondays — plan around both.

ddp.name: Dongdaemun Design Plaza (DDP)
ddp.blurb: Zaha Hadid’s flowing landmark and night market.
intro: The Dongdaemun Design Plaza, designed by Zaha Hadid, is a sweeping silver landmark of curves with barely a straight line — Seoul’s hub for design, exhibitions and fashion.
The surrounding Dongdaemun district is a round-the-clock shopping area, liveliest late at night.

Opened in 2014 on the site of a former baseball stadium, DDP is one of the world's largest column-free curved buildings, its skin formed of tens of thousands of individually shaped aluminium panels. It hosts Seoul Fashion Week and major design fairs, and the adjacent park preserves excavated Joseon-era ruins.
tips: It is most photogenic after dark, when the building and LED rose garden light up.
Exhibitions rotate — check what is on before you go.
The night-market fashion malls nearby run into the early hours.
The LED rose garden and the illuminated curves are the after-dark highlight; the Dongdaemun fashion malls nearby, like DOOTA, run into the early hours.

lotte-world-tower.name: Lotte World Tower
lotte-world-tower.blurb: Korea’s tallest tower — the Seoul Sky observation deck.
intro: Lotte World Tower in Jamsil is the tallest building in South Korea, with the Seoul Sky observation decks near the top for sweeping views over the city and the Han River.
At its base are a huge mall, an aquarium and a concert hall, with the Lotte World theme park next door.

Rising 555 m over 123 floors, Lotte World Tower opened in 2017 as one of the world's tallest buildings. Its Seoul Sky decks include a glass-floor skywalk, and the tapering silhouette was designed to echo traditional Korean ceramics and calligraphy brushes.
tips: Go on a clear day for the Seoul Sky view; sunset is popular.
Book Seoul Sky tickets ahead to skip the queue.
Seokchon Lake beside it is lovely in cherry-blossom season.
Buy Seoul Sky tickets online for a timed slot and go on a clear day near sunset; pair it with a spring cherry-blossom walk around Seokchon Lake below.

ikseondong.name: Ikseon-dong
ikseondong.blurb: Restored hanok alleys of cafes and boutiques.
intro: Ikseon-dong is a maze of narrow lanes where century-old hanok houses have been restored into cafes, dessert shops, boutiques and small restaurants.
It is a compact, atmospheric pocket that blends old architecture with a young, design-led scene.

The lanes date to a 1920s development often called one of Seoul's first planned hanok neighbourhoods. Long faded, they were revived from the 2010s into today's warren of cafes and boutiques, and the tight grid of alleys is easy — and fun — to lose yourself in.
tips: Come to wander slowly and cafe-hop — it is small but dense.
Weekday afternoons are calmer than weekends.
It is a short walk from Jongno-3-ga station and Insadong.
It's tiny and best explored on foot, spilling into the Nakwon and Insadong areas nearby; go on a weekday afternoon to beat the queues at the popular dessert cafes.

yonggungsa.name: Haedong Yonggungsa
yonggungsa.blurb: A rare Buddhist temple right on the sea.
intro: Haedong Yonggungsa is one of Korea’s few seaside temples, its shrines and pagodas built onto the rocks just above the waves on Busan’s northeast coast.
The mix of sea, cliffs and temple makes it especially striking at sunrise.

Founded in 1376 and rebuilt last century, the temple is reached by a path past twelve zodiac statues and a stairway of 108 steps down to the shrines above the waves. It's at its most magical at sunrise and during Buddha's Birthday, when lanterns line the approach.
tips: Sunrise and early morning are the most peaceful times.
There are many steps down to the temple and back up.
Combine it with the coastal spots on an east-Busan day.
There's no subway to the gate — take a bus or taxi from Haeundae or Centum. Pair it with the nearby Osiria resort area and Lotte World Adventure Busan.

taejongdae.name: Taejongdae
taejongdae.blurb: Cliff-top park with sea views and a lighthouse.
intro: Taejongdae is a forested coastal park on the southern tip of Busan’s Yeongdo island, ringed by dramatic sea cliffs, a lighthouse and viewpoints over open water.
A road train loops the park for those who would rather not walk the whole hilly circuit.

The park is named after King Taejong Muyeol of Silla, who is said to have admired the view here. Its cliffs drop to the Sinseon Rock platform and a pebble beach, and on the clearest days the Japanese island of Tsushima can appear on the horizon.
tips: Take the Danubi road train if you would rather not walk the hilly loop.
The observatory and lighthouse have the best views.
On clear days you can sometimes see distant islands.
The Danubi road train loops the hilly circuit with stops at the observatory and lighthouse; wear comfortable shoes for the steep paths down to the rocks and check the return times.

songdo.name: Songdo Beach
songdo.blurb: Historic beach with an air-cruise cable car.
intro: Songdo is one of Korea’s oldest public beaches, now best known for the Songdo Air Cruise cable car gliding out over the bay and a curving cloud-trail skywalk along the shore.
It is a relaxed, family-friendly alternative to busier Haeundae.

Opened in 1913, Songdo was Korea's first designated public beach. Today the Songdo Air Cruise cable car glides over the bay toward Amnam Park, and a curving cloud-trail skywalk — the Songdo Yonggung Suspension Bridge — reaches out to a small offshore islet.
tips: The cable car has standard and glass-floor ‘crystal’ cabins.
Walk the seaside skywalk for photos out over the water.
It is a short hop from Nampo-dong and Jagalchi.
The cable car has standard and glass-floor 'crystal' cabins — book ahead on busy weekends. It's a short hop from Nampo-dong and Jagalchi Market.

jusangjeolli.name: Jusangjeolli Cliffs
jusangjeolli.blurb: Hexagonal basalt columns above the sea.
intro: The Jusangjeolli Cliffs on Jeju’s south coast are a wall of dark, hexagonal basalt columns formed as lava met the sea, with waves crashing against the stacked stone.
A short boardwalk leads to viewpoints over the formation.

The pillars formed as lava from Hallasan met the cold sea and fractured into tall polygonal columns, some rising over 20 m. The site lies within the Jungmun resort area on Jeju's south coast and is protected as a natural monument.
tips: Rougher-sea days make the waves against the columns more dramatic.
It is an easy, flat walk from the parking area.
Pair it with the Jungmun resort area and Cheonjiyeon Waterfall nearby.
A flat cliff-top boardwalk links the viewpoints; the waves are most dramatic on windy, high-tide days, and it pairs well with the nearby Cheonjiyeon Waterfall and Jungmun Beach.

insadong.name: Insadong
insadong.blurb: Antiques, tea houses and traditional crafts.
intro: Insadong is Seoul’s traditional-culture street, lined with antique shops, art galleries, craft stores, tea houses and calligraphy studios.
Its main lane and side alleys are pedestrian-friendly and easy to browse on foot.

Long the city's antiques and art quarter, Insadong mixes traditional teahouses and shops selling hanji paper, ceramics and calligraphy brushes with modern galleries. The four-storey Ssamziegil complex spirals around an open courtyard of small studios.
tips: Duck into the side alleys for tea houses and hidden courtyards.
The Ssamziegil complex spirals upward with small craft shops.
It is an easy walk from Gyeongbokgung and Bukchon.
On weekends the main street becomes a car-free zone with performances and food stalls — look for kkul-tarae (dragon's-beard candy) and other traditional sweets being made by hand.

gwangjang-market.name: Gwangjang Market
gwangjang-market.blurb: One of Seoul’s oldest street-food markets.
intro: Gwangjang Market is one of Seoul’s oldest traditional markets, famous for its buzzing street-food alley.
Grab a stool for bindaetteok (mung-bean pancakes), mayak gimbap and other classics.

Opened in 1905, Gwangjang is one of Korea's first permanent markets. Alongside the food alley it's known for a big second-hand and vintage-fabric section upstairs, and its bindaetteok and mayak-gimbap stalls have turned it into a global food-tour favourite.
tips: Come hungry and share several dishes across stalls.
Lunchtime and early evening are liveliest.
Many food stalls prefer cash.
The food alley is liveliest from midday into the evening; carry some cash, and walk it off afterwards along the Cheonggyecheon stream a block away.

gwangalli.name: Gwangalli Beach
gwangalli.blurb: Beach with the Gwangan Bridge light show.
intro: Gwangalli is a relaxed city beach framed by the Gwangan ‘Diamond’ Bridge, whose nightly light show makes it Busan’s favourite after-dark spot.
A young strip of cafes, bars and seafood restaurants lines the sand.

The view is anchored by the Gwangan Bridge, a landmark suspension span that opened in 2003 and lights up after dark. The beach hosts Busan's big autumn fireworks festival and, on some weekends, drone light shows over the water.
tips: Come at night for the bridge light show, and drone shows on some weekends.
The cafe-and-bar strip is livelier than Haeundae’s.
It is a short subway hop from Haeundae.
The back-street cafes and bars buzz late; for the classic shot, sit on the sand facing the bridge after sunset. It's just one subway stop from Haeundae.

cheonjiyeon.name: Cheonjiyeon Waterfall
cheonjiyeon.blurb: Lush waterfall in the heart of Seogwipo.
intro: Cheonjiyeon Waterfall tumbles into a wide pool at the end of a short, lush trail in Seogwipo on Jeju’s south coast.
The subtropical gorge around it stays green year-round and is lit at night.

The name means 'sky-connected pond'. The subtropical gorge shelters protected plants and is a rare natural habitat of the endangered marbled eel — both designated natural monuments — and floodlights make it a popular evening walk.
tips: The walk in is short, flat and stroller-friendly.
Evenings bring illuminations along the path.
Pair it with Jusangjeolli and the Jungmun area nearby.
The flat, stroller-friendly path in takes only about 15 minutes; combine it with the nearby Cheonjeyeon falls, the Jusangjeolli cliffs and the Seogwipo Maeil Olle Market.

manjanggul.name: Manjanggul Cave
manjanggul.blurb: A vast UNESCO lava tube you can walk through.
intro: Manjanggul is one of the world’s finest lava tubes and part of Jeju’s UNESCO World Heritage listing, formed by flowing volcanic lava.
An open section leads through the tunnel to a towering lava column.

Formed a few hundred thousand years ago, Manjanggul runs about 7.4 km, of which around 1 km is open to visitors. That section ends at a lava column about 7.6 m tall — one of the world's largest — and the cave shelters a colony of bats.
tips: It stays cool inside year-round — bring a light layer.
The floor is uneven and damp; wear grippy shoes.
It is on the east side, near Seongsan.
It holds a steady temperature near 10°C all year, so bring a jacket even in summer. The floor is dark, damp and uneven — wear grippy closed-toe shoes, and note it can close for conservation.

bulguksa.name: Bulguksa Temple
intro: Bulguksa is a masterpiece of Silla-era Buddhist art and a UNESCO World Heritage site, with stone terraces, bridges and two celebrated pagodas.
It is the centrepiece of a visit to Gyeongju, Korea’s ancient capital.

Built in its grand form in 751 during the Silla kingdom, Bulguksa is famed for the Dabotap and Seokgatap pagodas and its stone stairway 'bridges'. UNESCO listed it in 1995 together with the Seokguram Grotto on the mountain above.
tips: Pair it with the Seokguram Grotto up the same mountain.
Mornings are quietest and best for photos.
Autumn colour around the temple is spectacular.
A short bus ride up the mountain reaches Seokguram Grotto and its celebrated seated Buddha — do the two together. Bulguksa is a working temple, so dress modestly and keep quiet inside the halls.

cheomseongdae.name: Cheomseongdae Observatory
cheomseongdae.blurb: One of Asia’s oldest surviving observatories.
intro: Cheomseongdae is a bottle-shaped stone tower from the Silla kingdom, regarded as one of the oldest surviving astronomical observatories in Asia.
It stands among royal tombs and seasonal flower fields in central Gyeongju.

Built under Queen Seondeok in the Silla kingdom, Cheomseongdae's stones are arranged in symbolic numbers tied to the days and months of the year, and it is designated a National Treasure of Korea — often called one of Asia's oldest surviving observatories.
tips: The surrounding Wolseong parkland is lovely at dusk.
It is floodlit and photogenic after dark.
Combine it with Donggung Palace and Wolji Pond next door.
It's floodlit after dark amid a broad park of tombs and seasonal flower fields; walk on to Donggung Palace and Wolji Pond, which mirror their lights on the water at night.

wolji.name: Donggung Palace & Wolji Pond
wolji.blurb: Silla palace ruins mirrored in a night-lit pond.
intro: Donggung Palace and Wolji Pond (formerly Anapji) are the restored grounds of a Silla royal pleasure garden, most magical after dark.
Illuminated pavilions reflect in the still water — Gyeongju’s signature night view.

The pond was dug in 674 as part of the Silla crown prince's East Palace. Excavations in the 1970s recovered thousands of artefacts — from carved dice to a wooden boat, now shown at the Gyeongju National Museum — and roof tiles found here corrected its old name Anapji to Wolji, 'moon pond'.
tips: Come after sunset for the famous reflections.
It is a short walk from Cheomseongdae.
Check the closing time so you do not miss the evening view.
Arrive before sunset to catch the pavilions in daylight and then lit up in the water; it's steps from Cheomseongdae and Daereungwon, and evening entry closes early — check the time.

cheonggyecheon.name: Cheonggyecheon Stream
cheonggyecheon.blurb: A restored stream cutting through downtown Seoul.
intro: Cheonggyecheon is a restored stream that runs through the heart of Seoul, sunk below street level as a long walking park.
Once buried under a highway, it is now a cool, green escape with stepping stones, fountains and seasonal light displays.

The roughly 11 km stream was buried under an elevated highway in the 1970s, then uncovered and restored in 2005 as a public waterway — a landmark of Seoul's urban renewal. It runs from Cheonggye Plaza past a series of bridges toward the Han River.
tips: It is a refreshing walk on a hot day — the water keeps it cooler.
Evenings bring lantern and light installations, especially in winter.
Start near Gwanghwamun / Cheonggye Plaza and follow it east.
Steps lead down from street level every block or so; a winter lantern festival and seasonal displays light it up (check the dates), and the water makes it a cool shortcut on a hot day.

huinnyeoul.name: Huinnyeoul Culture Village
huinnyeoul.blurb: Whitewashed lanes on a seaside cliff.
intro: Huinnyeoul Culture Village clings to a cliff on Busan’s Yeongdo island, its white houses and narrow lanes looking straight out over the sea.
A coastal path runs below the village along the water’s edge.

The name means 'white rippling water', for streams that once ran down the cliffs. Nicknamed Busan's Santorini, the tightly stacked houses became famous as a film and drama location, and the seaside path below runs past little cafes carved into the base of the cliff.
tips: Walk both the upper lanes and the lower seaside path.
It is a residential area — keep noise down.
Combine it with Taejongdae on Yeongdo.
Walk both the upper lanes and the lower waterfront path; it's a lived-in neighbourhood, so keep your voice down, and combine it with Taejongdae and Jagalchi on Yeongdo.

udo.name: Udo Island
udo.blurb: A tiny island of beaches and coastal cycling.
intro: Udo (‘Cow Island’) is a small islet off Jeju’s east coast, reached by a short ferry and best explored by bike, scooter or the island bus.
White-and-turquoise beaches, low stone walls and sea views make it a relaxed half-day trip.

Udo is ringed by scenic spots like the Seobin Baeksa coral-sand beach and the Udobong peak, and its waters are still worked by haenyeo divers. The island is also famous for peanut ice cream, made from peanuts grown in its volcanic soil.
tips: Take the ferry from near Seongsan; it is a short crossing.
Rent a bike or electric scooter to loop the island.
Go early to beat day-trip crowds in peak season.
Ferries leave from Seongsanpo and Jongdal harbours; private cars are allowed only in limited cases, so most visitors rent a bike, electric scooter or cart, or take the island bus.

jeonju-hanok.name: Jeonju Hanok Village
jeonju-hanok.blurb: Korea’s best-known hanok village and food capital.
intro: Jeonju Hanok Village is a large, well-preserved neighbourhood of traditional hanok houses in the city that gave the world bibimbap.
Its lanes are packed with tea houses, craft workshops, hanbok rentals and street food.

With more than 700 hanok houses it is Korea's largest such village, set beside the Gyeonggijeon shrine and the historic Jeondong Catholic Church. Jeonju is a UNESCO City of Gastronomy — the home of bibimbap and lively makgeolli alleys.
tips: Try Jeonju-style bibimbap and the local street food.
Rent a hanbok to wander the lanes.
It is an easy trip from Seoul by fast train and bus.
Come hungry: try Jeonju bibimbap, the famous PNB choco pie and Gyodong's street snacks. It's busiest on weekends, and the short climb up Omokdae gives a rooftop view over the tiled roofs.

gyeonggijeon.name: Gyeonggijeon Shrine
gyeonggijeon.blurb: Serene shrine beside the hanok village.
intro: Gyeonggijeon is a tranquil walled shrine holding a portrait of King Taejo, founder of the Joseon dynasty, right beside Jeonju Hanok Village.
Its bamboo groves and old halls are a calm counterpoint to the busy lanes outside.

Built in 1410, Gyeonggijeon enshrines a royal portrait of King Taejo, founder of the Joseon dynasty. Its grounds also hold the Royal Portrait Museum and a repository that once safeguarded the dynasty's official annals — a UNESCO documentary-heritage record.
tips: It pairs naturally with a Jeonju Hanok Village visit.
The bamboo grove and rear gardens are the highlight.
The nearby Jeondong Catholic Cathedral is worth a look.
It's a calm pause beside busy Jeonju Hanok Village and a favourite hanbok photo backdrop; pair it with the neighbouring Jeondong Catholic Cathedral.

gyeongpo.name: Gyeongpo Beach
gyeongpo.blurb: Gangneung’s wide beach and coffee scene.
intro: Gyeongpo is Gangneung’s long, wide East Sea beach, backed by pine groves, a scenic lake and one of Korea’s best-known coffee cultures.
It is the summer favourite of the east coast, an easy fast-train ride from Seoul.

Gyeongpo pairs a long East Sea beach with Gyeongpo Lake and the historic Gyeongpodae pavilion — a Joseon-era spot famed in legend for seeing five moons at once. Nearby, Anmok's 'coffee street' helped spark Korea's specialty-coffee boom.
tips: The cafe strip along Anmok beach is famous for coffee.
Gyeongpo Lake beside the beach is lovely for a cherry-blossom walk.
Summer weekends are busy — arrive early.
Walk or cycle the lake loop, loveliest under spring cherry blossoms. The beach is the east coast's summer favourite and an easy fast-train ride from Seoul, so arrive early on weekends.

jeongdongjin.name: Jeongdongjin
jeongdongjin.blurb: Famous sunrise beach with a seaside railway.
intro: Jeongdongjin is a small east-coast town known for sunrises over the sea and a railway station that sits right on the beach.
A hilltop sail-shaped hotel and an hourglass park add to its quirky charm.

The name marks the point 'due east' of Seoul's old palace, and the beachside station — once ranked among the world's closest to the sea — became famous through a 1990s TV drama. The hilltop Sun Cruise resort is even built in the shape of a ship.
tips: It is a classic spot to watch the New Year sunrise.
The station is one of the closest to the sea anywhere.
Reachable by train down the east coast from Gangneung.
It's a classic New Year sunrise spot, packed on 1 January; ride the slow east-coast train or the sea-view rail bike, and the nearby Hourglass Park turns its giant hourglass once a year.

hwaseong.name: Hwaseong Fortress
hwaseong.blurb: UNESCO fortress walls circling old Suwon.
intro: Hwaseong is a grand Joseon-era fortress wall that rings the old centre of Suwon, a UNESCO World Heritage site of gates, watchtowers and floodgates.
You can walk the full circuit of the walls for ever-changing views over the city.

Completed in 1796 under King Jeongjo, Hwaseong wraps about 5.7 km of wall around old Suwon and blended Eastern and Western military design of its era — reasons it joined the UNESCO list in 1997. The Hwaseong Haenggung palace inside hosts changing-of-the-guard and martial-arts shows.
tips: Walk a section of the wall between the grand gates.
A trolley and archery experiences run inside the fortress.
It is a short train ride south of Seoul.
Walk a stretch between the Janganmun and Paldalmun gates, ride the dragon trolley, or try archery at the fortress — it's a short train or bus ride south of Seoul to Suwon.

daereungwon.name: Daereungwon Tomb Complex
daereungwon.blurb: Grassy royal burial mounds of ancient Silla.
intro: Daereungwon is a park of large grassy burial mounds holding the tombs of Silla kings and nobles in the heart of Gyeongju.
One mound, Cheonmachong, is open inside to show excavated treasures and a famous painted saddle flap.

The park holds 23 large earthen mounds raised over Silla kings and nobles. Cheonmachong, excavated in the 1970s, gave up a gold crown and the 'Heavenly Horse' painting that names it, while the neighbouring Hwangnam Daechong is the largest tomb of all.
tips: Cheonmachong is the one tomb you can step inside.
The mounds are lovely at dusk and in cherry-blossom season.
It is walking distance from Cheomseongdae and the Hwangnidan-gil street.

It's floodlit and romantic at dusk and lovely in cherry-blossom season, and sits steps from the Cheomseongdae observatory and the trendy Hwangnidan-gil cafe street — an easy walking loop of old Gyeongju.

jaman.name: Jaman Mural Village
jaman.blurb: A hillside of alleys covered in murals.
intro: Jaman Mural Village climbs a hill on the edge of Jeonju Hanok Village, its narrow lanes and old walls painted with colourful murals.
Small cafes and craft shops tuck in between the artworks.
tips: It is a short but steep walk up from the hanok village.
Great for photos and a quiet coffee away from the crowds.
Wear comfortable shoes for the slopes.

ojukheon.name: Ojukheon
ojukheon.blurb: One of Korea’s oldest surviving wooden houses.
intro: Ojukheon in Gangneung is the birthplace of the Joseon scholar Yi I and his mother, the artist Shin Saimdang — both featured on Korean banknotes.
It is one of the oldest surviving wooden homes in the country, set in a quiet garden of black bamboo.

Built in the early Joseon period, Ojukheon is one of Korea's oldest surviving wooden houses. Here the artist Shin Saimdang raised her son, the Confucian scholar Yi I (Yulgok) — a mother and son so revered that both appear on today's banknotes, a pairing unique in Korea.
tips: Look for the black-bamboo grove that gives the house its name.
There is a small museum on the grounds.
Pair it with Gyeongpo Beach and lake nearby.
The black-bamboo grove behind the house gives it its name; there's a small museum and memorial hall on the grounds, and it pairs with Gyeongpo Beach and lake nearby.

haenggung.name: Hwaseong Haenggung Palace
haenggung.blurb: The detached palace inside Hwaseong Fortress.
intro: Hwaseong Haenggung was a temporary palace where the king stayed when visiting Suwon — the largest of Joseon’s detached palaces, set within Hwaseong Fortress.
Restored courtyards and halls host changing-of-the-guard and martial-arts performances.

Hwaseong Haenggung served King Jeongjo on visits to his father's tomb, and in 1795 it hosted the lavish 60th-birthday feast for his mother — an event re-enacted today. The grandest of Joseon's detached palaces, it has featured in many historical dramas.
tips: Check the schedule for guard-ceremony and martial-arts shows.
Combine it with a walk on the Hwaseong walls.
It is a short train ride south of Seoul.
Time your visit for the guard-changing and martial-arts shows, try a traditional-craft experience, and walk straight out onto the Hwaseong fortress walls above.

starfield-coex.name: Starfield Library (COEX)
starfield-coex.blurb: A soaring open library inside COEX Mall.
intro: The Starfield Library is a vast, open two-storey library at the heart of the COEX Mall in Gangnam, with towering shelves that have made it one of Seoul’s most photographed spots.
The mall around it holds shops, an aquarium and the SMTOWN K-pop complex.

Opened in 2017, the library fills a sunken plaza with two soaring walls of shelves holding tens of thousands of books and magazines, all free to browse. It anchors COEX — one of Korea's largest underground malls — alongside an aquarium and the SMTOWN K-pop complex.
tips: It is free to enter and browse.
Weekday mornings are quietest for photos.
K-pop fans can visit SMTOWN in the same complex.
Entry is free; visit on a weekday morning for photos without the crowds. The mall connects underground toward the Bongeunsa temple and trade-centre area.

oryukdo.name: Oryukdo Skywalk
oryukdo.blurb: Glass-floor walkway over the sea cliffs.
intro: The Oryukdo Skywalk is a horseshoe-shaped glass walkway jutting out from the cliffs at the southern tip of Busan, above the rocky Oryukdo islets.
It marks the point where Korea’s South Sea meets the East Sea.
tips: You put on slippers over your shoes to protect the glass.
Clear days give the best views of the islets.
The nearby Igidae coastal trail is worth the extra time.

seoraksan.name: Seoraksan National Park
seoraksan.blurb: Granite peaks, temples and autumn colour.
intro: Seoraksan is Korea’s most famous national park — dramatic granite peaks, valleys and temples near the east-coast city of Sokcho.
A cable car climbs toward Gwongeumseong fortress, and trails of every level fan out from Sinheungsa temple.

A UNESCO Biosphere Reserve, Seoraksan rises to Daecheongbong at 1,708 m. Favourites include the Ulsanbawi rock ridge, Biryong Falls and the giant bronze Buddha at Sinheungsa temple, and it is usually Korea's first mountain to turn colour each autumn.
tips: Autumn foliage is spectacular but very busy — go early.
Take the cable car for big views without the full climb.
Bring layers; mountain weather changes fast.
The cable car and gentle valley trails suit most visitors, while Ulsanbawi is a strenuous stair climb. Autumn weekends are extremely crowded — start at dawn or come midweek.

abai.name: Abai Village
abai.blurb: A seaside village reached by a hand-pulled ferry.
intro: Abai Village in Sokcho was settled by refugees from the north and is famous for its hand-pulled ‘gaetbae’ raft-ferry across the channel.
It is known for Abai sundae and squid dishes, and as a filming spot for hit Korean dramas.

The village grew after the Korean War, when people from the north's Hamgyong region settled here expecting to return home. Its hand-pulled 'gaetbae' cable ferry and its starring role in the hit drama 'Autumn in My Heart' made it famous, and Abai-style sundae reflects those northern roots.
tips: Ride the hand-pulled ferry across the inlet.
Try Abai sundae (stuffed sausage) and squid sundae.
Combine it with Sokcho Beach and the fish market.
Ride the gaetbae across the channel and try Abai and squid sundae; combine it with Sokcho's fish market, the beach and nearby Seoraksan.

ihwa.name: Ihwa Mural Village
ihwa.blurb: A steep hillside of murals near Naksan.
intro: Ihwa Mural Village climbs the slope below Naksan Park, its stairways and walls brightened with murals and art installations.
From the top there are wide views over the rooftops of old Seoul.
tips: It is a residential area — keep noise down and respect homes.
Combine it with a walk on the Naksan section of the old city wall.
Wear comfortable shoes for the steep lanes.

igidae.name: Igidae Coastal Walk
igidae.blurb: A rugged cliffside trail along the sea.
intro: Igidae is a coastal park in Busan with a rocky cliff trail and a suspension bridge, looking across the water to the Gwangan Bridge and the Haeundae skyline.
It links along the shore toward the Oryukdo Skywalk.

Part of Busan's Galmaetgil coastal trail, Igidae's cliff path skirts wave-carved rock formations and a swaying suspension bridge, with the Gwangan Bridge and Haeundae skyline across Suyeong Bay. Its name comes from a local legend of two kisaeng entertainers.
tips: Wear good shoes — parts are rocky with stairs.
The Gwangan Bridge views are best in the late afternoon.
You can walk on toward the Oryukdo Skywalk.
Wear grippy shoes for the rocky steps and boardwalks; the Gwangan Bridge glows best in late afternoon and after dark, and you can walk on to the Oryukdo Skywalk.

hyeopjae.name: Hyeopjae Beach
hyeopjae.blurb: White sand and turquoise water on Jeju’s west.
intro: Hyeopjae is one of Jeju’s prettiest beaches — white sand, shallow turquoise water and a view of Biyangdo island offshore.
The Hallim Park gardens and caves sit right next door.

The beach's bright colour comes from crushed white shells and coral mixed through the sand, and it looks out to the small volcanic island of Biyangdo. Right next door, Hallim Park packs in subtropical gardens and the Hyeopjae and Ssangyong lava caves.
tips: The water is shallow and calm — good for families.
Sunset over Biyangdo island is lovely.
Pair it with Hallim Park next door.
The water is shallow and calm — good for families and paddling. Come for sunset behind Biyangdo, and picnic under the pine grove that backs the sand.

nambu-market.name: Jeonju Nambu Market
nambu-market.blurb: A traditional market with a youthful night hall.
intro: Nambu Market is Jeonju’s big traditional market — busy by day with produce and street food, and known for its ‘Youth Mall’ of young vendors upstairs.
On weekend nights a night market fills the aisles with food stalls.
tips: Come hungry — it is one of Jeonju’s best street-food spots.
Check for the weekend night market.
It is a short walk from the Hanok Village.

national-museum-korea.name: National Museum of Korea
national-museum-korea.blurb: Korea's largest museum — free entry to millennia of art and history.
intro: The National Museum of Korea in Yongsan is the country's flagship museum, tracing Korean history from prehistory through the Joseon era across vast, well-labelled galleries.
General admission is free and English signage makes it easy for first-time visitors.

Opened at its Yongsan home in 2005, it ranks among the world's most-visited museums, holding hundreds of thousands of objects. Highlights include the gold crowns of Silla, the serene Pensive Bodhisattvas, and the towering Gyeongcheonsa stone pagoda rising in the central hall.
tips: General admission is free; some special exhibitions are ticketed.
Don't miss the Pensive Bodhisattva room and the tall stone pagoda in the main hall.
It sits inside Yongsan Family Park — pair it with a riverside walk.
Allow at least half a day; the reflecting-pond grounds and Yongsan Family Park make a good riverside pairing, and it's a short walk from Ichon Station.

seoul-forest.name: Seoul Forest
seoul-forest.blurb: A big riverside park with a deer enclosure, gardens and café streets nearby.
intro: Seoul Forest is a large park east of the city centre, with wooded walking paths, a deer enclosure, water gardens and open lawns popular for picnics.
It sits beside the Han River and the trendy Seongsu café district.

Opened in 2005 on land that had been a royal hunting ground and later a racecourse, Seoul Forest is one of the city's largest parks, split into themed zones — an eco-forest with roaming deer, wetlands, and riverside lawns beside the Han River.
tips: Free to enter and open year-round.
Walk or cycle the Han River path straight from the park.
Seongsu's cafés and pop-up stores are a short walk away.
It's free and open year-round; rent a bike to join the Han River path, and the Seongsu café-and-pop-up district (home to the KWANGYA store) is a short walk away.

beomeosa.name: Beomeosa Temple
beomeosa.blurb: A serene Silla-era temple on the wooded slopes of Geumjeongsan.
intro: Beomeosa is one of Busan's most important Buddhist temples, founded in the Silla era on the forested slopes of Geumjeongsan.
Its halls, stone pagoda and mountain setting feel a world away from the city's beaches.

Founded in 678 during the Silla kingdom, Beomeosa is a head temple of the Jogye Buddhist order, known for its spring wisteria and its Iljumun gate and Daeungjeon hall. It runs templestay programs for visitors who want to stay overnight.
tips: Combine it with a hike on Geumjeongsan or a walk along the old fortress wall.
Dress modestly — it's an active temple.
Take the subway to Beomeosa Station, then a short bus or uphill walk.
From Beomeosa Station take a short bus or uphill walk to the gate; combine it with a Geumjeongsan hike or the old fortress wall, and dress modestly as it's an active temple.

songjeong-beach.name: Songjeong Beach
songjeong-beach.blurb: A relaxed sandy beach popular for beginner surfing, just east of Haeundae.
intro: Songjeong is a calmer, more local beach just east of Haeundae, with gentle waves that make it Busan's favourite spot for first-time surfers.
Surf shops, cafés and the scenic Blueline Park coastal rail are all close by.

A gently curving bay sheltered from big swells, Songjeong is Busan's go-to learn-to-surf beach, dotted with surf schools and board rentals. The restored Songjeong Station is now the start of the Blueline Park beach train and sky capsules running toward Cheongsapo and Haeundae.
tips: Surf schools rent boards and run lessons in season.
The Blueline Park coastal rail runs between Songjeong and Haeundae.
It's quieter than Haeundae, especially on weekdays.
Surf schools run lessons and rent gear in season; it's calmer and more local than Haeundae, and the Blueline Park train makes a scenic hop along the old coastal railway.

seopjikoji.name: Seopjikoji
seopjikoji.blurb: A grassy coastal cape with low cliffs, a lighthouse and spring canola fields.
intro: Seopjikoji is a grassy cape on Jeju's eastern coast, with easy paths along low cliffs, a white lighthouse and views back to Seongsan Ilchulbong.
In spring the surrounding fields turn bright yellow with canola blossom.

'Koji' means cape in the Jeju dialect, and this grassy headland is dotted with landmarks — including the Glass House and Genius Loci pavilions designed by the architect Tadao Ando. It has been a backdrop for many Korean dramas and films.
tips: Pair it with Seongsan Ilchulbong, which is close by.
Spring canola season and clear days are the most scenic.
The walk out to the lighthouse is easy and mostly flat.
The flat loop out to the red-and-white lighthouse is easy; canola blossom peaks in spring, and clear days give the best views back to Seongsan Ilchulbong next door.

seokguram.name: Seokguram Grotto
seokguram.blurb: A UNESCO granite grotto sheltering a serene seated Buddha above Bulguksa.
intro: Seokguram is a Silla-era stone grotto high on Tohamsan above Bulguksa, sheltering a magnificent seated Buddha ringed by carved guardians and bodhisattvas.
It is a UNESCO World Heritage Site, listed together with Bulguksa temple.

Built in the Silla kingdom alongside Bulguksa, the granite grotto was engineered so that — before modern glazing — the seated Buddha caught the sunrise over the East Sea. Its domed ceiling and ring of relief carvings are counted among the peaks of Silla Buddhist art.
tips: Visit it together with Bulguksa — they share the same mountain and heritage listing.
The main Buddha is viewed through glass to protect it, and photography inside is restricted.
Sunrise over the eastern ridges is famous here.
A shuttle bus or a forest trail links it with Bulguksa down the mountain. The hall is quiet and reverent — no photos of the Buddha, and dress modestly.

lotte-world.name: Lotte World
lotte-world.blurb: A huge theme park with an indoor 'Adventure' dome and an outdoor 'Magic Island' by a lake.
intro: Lotte World is one of Seoul's biggest theme parks — a covered indoor section that's great whatever the weather, plus an outdoor 'Magic Island' with rides around a lake.
It's easy to reach by subway and pairs with Lotte World Tower and Seokchon Lake right next door.

Opened in 1989, Lotte World holds a Guinness record as the world's largest indoor theme park — its glass-roofed Adventure hall runs whatever the weather, with the outdoor Magic Island castle on Seokchon Lake alongside. There's also an ice rink and a folk museum on site.
tips: Weekdays are far quieter than weekends.
It's right by Jamsil Station and Lotte World Tower.
The indoor area is a lifesaver on a rainy or very hot day.
Visit on a weekday to dodge the queues; after-4pm and single-ride tickets exist, and it links directly to Jamsil Station, Lotte World Tower and Seokchon Lake.

namdaemun-market.name: Namdaemun Market
namdaemun-market.blurb: Korea's largest traditional market — street food, goods and bargains.
intro: Namdaemun is Korea's largest traditional market, a maze of alleys packed with clothes, kitchenware, accessories and some of Seoul's best street food.
It runs day and night and sits right by Namdaemun gate and Myeongdong.

With roots reaching back more than 600 years to the early Joseon dynasty, Namdaemun is Korea's oldest and largest traditional market — thousands of shops selling clothes, glasses, kitchenware and more, many trading through the night for wholesale buyers.
tips: Come hungry — the food alleys are the highlight (try the hotteok and kalguksu).
Haggling is normal for goods, less so for food.
It's a short walk from Myeongdong and Seoul Station.
Dive into the food alleys for hotteok, the 'noodle alley' kalguksu and galchi-jorim (braised hairtail); many stalls prefer cash, and it's an easy walk from Myeongdong and Seoul Station.

yongdusan.name: Yongdusan Park & Busan Tower
yongdusan.blurb: A hilltop park crowned by Busan Tower, with panoramic views over the port.
intro: Yongdusan Park sits on a hill in the middle of downtown Busan, topped by Busan Tower with sweeping views over the harbour and city.
It's steps from Nampo-dong, Gukje Market and the Jagalchi fish market.
tips: Go up the tower near sunset for the best light.
Escalators from Nampo-dong save you the climb.
Pair it with Gukje Market and Jagalchi nearby.

cheonjeyeon.name: Cheonjeyeon Waterfall
cheonjeyeon.blurb: A lush three-tier waterfall with a scenic 'Fairy Bridge' near Jungmun.
intro: Cheonjeyeon is a three-tier waterfall set in dense subtropical forest on Jeju's south coast, linked by shady paths and the ornate Seonimgyo 'fairy bridge'.
It sits beside the Jungmun resort area.

The name means 'pond of the emperor of heaven', from a legend of seven fairies who bathed here — a story painted on the arched Seonimgyo 'Seven Nymphs Bridge' overhead. The lush gorge is a protected natural-monument forest beside the Jungmun resort complex.
tips: Don't mix it up with Cheonjiyeon — this is the three-tier one near Jungmun.
The top tier flows mainly after rain; the lower tiers are reliable.
Combine it with Jungmun beach and the Jusangjeolli cliffs.
The top tier flows mainly after rain while the lower tiers run year-round; don't confuse it with Cheonjiyeon, and pair it with Jungmun beach and the Jusangjeolli cliffs.

sanbangsan.name: Sanbangsan
sanbangsan.blurb: A dramatic bell-shaped lava dome with a cliffside cave temple and sea views.
intro: Sanbangsan is a striking bell-shaped lava dome on Jeju's southwest coast, with a cliff grotto temple (Sanbanggulsa) part-way up and wide views over the sea.
The Yongmeori coast right below makes an easy half-day.

The dome is a lava plug that hardened in a volcanic vent — by legend, a peak torn from Hallasan. The Sanbanggulsa grotto shrine sits in a natural cave part-way up, and the rare cliff plants on its slopes are protected as a natural monument.
tips: The climb to the grotto temple is short but steep.
Pair it with the Yongmeori coastal walk below.
It's especially pretty with the canola fields in spring.
The climb to the grotto is short but steep and stepped; pair it with the Yongmeori coast just below, and it's ringed by bright canola fields in spring.

woljeonggyo.name: Woljeonggyo Bridge
woljeonggyo.blurb: A beautifully reconstructed Silla-era covered wooden bridge, stunning at night.
intro: Woljeonggyo is a reconstructed Silla-era wooden bridge over the Namcheon stream in Gyeongju, with an elegant pavilion-roofed walkway.
It's most photogenic in the evening, lit up and reflected in the water.

First built in 760 during the Silla kingdom and reconstructed in recent years, Woljeonggyo is a covered wooden footbridge spanning the Namcheon by the old Wolseong palace site, its pavilions and painted eaves reflected in the water.
tips: Come after dark for the illuminated reflection.
It's an easy walk or bike ride from Gyeongju's royal tomb park.
Free to cross and open into the evening.
It's floodlit after dark for the classic mirror-reflection photo; free to cross, it's an easy walk or bike ride from Gyeongju's tomb park and the Gyochon traditional village.

incheon-chinatown.name: Incheon Chinatown
incheon-chinatown.blurb: Korea's largest Chinatown — birthplace of jjajangmyeon, with painted alleys and street snacks.
intro: Incheon Chinatown, right by the port, is Korea's oldest and largest Chinatown — a colourful maze of Chinese restaurants, bakeries and mural-lined stairways.
It's the birthplace of jjajangmyeon (black-bean noodles), and the Jjajangmyeon Museum tells the story.

The quarter grew after the port opened to foreign trade in 1883 and Chinese merchants settled here. Highlights today include the Samgukji murals retelling the Romance of the Three Kingdoms, the Jjajangmyeon Museum in a historic restaurant, and the adjoining Songwol-dong 'fairy-tale village'.
tips: Try jjajangmyeon and freshly-steamed gonggal-ppang bread.
Walk up to the Samgukji mural street and the fairy-tale village next door.
It's a short walk from Incheon Station on Line 1.
Arrive hungry for jjajangmyeon and hollow gonggal-ppang bread. It's right by Incheon Station at the end of Line 1, and pairs with the Wolmido waterfront a short ride away.

songdo-central-park.name: Songdo Central Park
songdo-central-park.blurb: A sleek waterfront park with a saltwater canal, framed by Songdo's skyline.
intro: Songdo Central Park is the green heart of Incheon's futuristic Songdo district — a landscaped park built around a seawater canal, with skyscrapers rising on every side.
You can rent a pedal boat or hop on a water taxi along the canal.

Opened in 2009 at the centre of the reclaimed Songdo International Business District, the park is built around a 1.8 km saltwater canal drawn from the sea — a first for a Korean park — and ringed by landmarks like the sail-shaped Tri-bowl hall and the G-Tower.
tips: It's especially striking at night when the towers light up.
Rent a boat on the canal, or walk the full loop.
Reachable on Incheon subway Line 1.
Rent a pedal boat or water taxi on the canal, or walk the full loop; it glows after dark when the towers light up, and it's on Incheon subway Line 1.

wolmido.name: Wolmido
wolmido.blurb: A breezy seaside boardwalk with rides, cafés, seagulls and sunset views.
intro: Wolmido is Incheon's seaside playground — a waterfront promenade lined with cafés, an old-school amusement area, and boats where seagulls follow you for snacks.
It's a favourite for a sunset stroll and fresh seafood.

Once a strategic point in the 1950 Incheon Landing, the former tidal island is now linked to shore and lined with a 'Culture Street' promenade. The retro My Land amusement park, the Wolmi Sea Train loop and a traditional park sit alongside its raw-fish restaurants.
tips: Feeding the seagulls from the ferry deck is a Wolmido tradition.
Come for sunset and stay for the seaside cafés.
A short bus ride from Incheon Station.
Feeding the gulls that trail the harbour ferries is a Wolmido tradition; come for sunset, and it's a short bus ride from Incheon Station — an easy add-on to the Chinatown.

eurwangni-beach.name: Eurwangni Beach
eurwangni-beach.blurb: A sandy sunset beach on Yeongjong Island, minutes from Incheon Airport.
intro: Eurwangni is a gentle sandy beach on Yeongjong Island, just minutes from Incheon Airport — a handy first or last stop, or an easy escape from Seoul.
It's known for shallow water, seafood restaurants and west-coast sunsets.
tips: Great for a layover or your first or last night near the airport.
Sunset here is the highlight.
Pair it with nearby Muui Island.

war-memorial.name: War Memorial of Korea
war-memorial.blurb: A vast, free museum of Korean military history with an outdoor weapons park.
intro: The War Memorial of Korea in Yongsan is a large, free museum tracing Korea's military history from ancient times through the Korean War, with moving memorial halls.
Its outdoor plaza displays tanks, aircraft and ships that kids and history buffs love.

Opened in 1994 on a former army-headquarters site, the museum runs across six indoor exhibition halls plus a vast outdoor park of tanks, aircraft and warships. Its Memorial Hall records the names of the fallen, including the UN allies of the Korean War.
tips: General admission is free.
The outdoor aircraft-and-tank park is a hit with kids.
It's near Itaewon and Samgakji Station.
General admission is free; allow a couple of hours, don't miss the outdoor hardware park with kids, and it's near Itaewon and Samgakji Station.

banpo-hangang.name: Banpo Hangang Park
banpo-hangang.blurb: A Han River park famous for the Banpo Bridge Moonlight Rainbow Fountain.
intro: Banpo Hangang Park stretches along the Han River beside Banpo Bridge, home to the Moonlight Rainbow Fountain — a light-and-water show that arcs off the bridge on summer evenings.
By day it's a favourite for picnics, bikes and convenience-store ramyeon by the water.

The Moonlight Rainbow Fountain runs along about 1,140 m of Banpo Bridge — recognised as the world's longest bridge fountain — shooting water and coloured light in shows set to music on spring-to-autumn evenings. Nearby, the Some Sevit floating islands light up the river.
tips: Check the fountain show times before you go — it's seasonal and runs in the evening.
Grab ramyeon and snacks from the riverside convenience store.
Rent a bike or a picnic mat and relax like the locals.
Check the show schedule — it's seasonal and evenings only; grab ramyeon at the riverside convenience store, rent a mat or bike, and settle on the grass like the locals.

seomun-market.name: Seomun Market
seomun-market.blurb: One of Korea's largest and oldest traditional markets — a huge day market that turns into a buzzing night food street.
intro: Seomun Market is one of Korea's largest and oldest traditional markets, in the heart of Daegu, with countless stalls of textiles, homeware and everything in between.
After dark the night market fires up and the aisles fill with food carts serving Daegu specialities under a canopy of lights.

Its roots reach back some 600 years to a Joseon-era market once counted among the country's three greatest. Today it's a warren of textile and goods stalls, and its night market — one of Korea's most famous — draws crowds for street food after dark.
tips: Come hungry after sunset — the night market runs into the evening with street food galore.
Try Daegu specialities like napjak-mandu (flat dumplings) and grilled makchang.
It's easy to reach on the Daegu Metro; the nearest stop is Seomun Market Station.
Come after sunset for the night market; try Daegu specialities like napjak-mandu (flat dumplings) and grilled makchang, and ride the Metro to Seomun Market Station.

apsan-park.name: Apsan Park
apsan-park.blurb: A forested mountain park on the city's edge, with a cable car up to a sweeping view over Daegu.
intro: Apsan Park spreads across the wooded slopes south of Daegu, laced with hiking trails, small temples and a cable car.
The observatory near the top offers one of the best city panoramas in the country — Daegu laid out below, especially at sunset and after dark.
tips: Ride the Apsan Cable Car up if you'd rather skip the climb to the observatory.
Time it for late afternoon to catch the city lights coming on.
It's a short taxi or bus ride from central Daegu.

mudeungsan.name: Mudeungsan National Park
mudeungsan.blurb: Gwangju's beloved national-park mountain, known for gentle ridgeline trails and dramatic rock columns near the top.
intro: Mudeungsan rises right behind Gwangju — a national park of forested ridges and famous columnar-rock formations near the summit.
Well-graded trails make it a favourite day hike, with wide views back over the city.

Designated a national park in 2013, Mudeungsan — its name means 'mountain without equal' — is crowned by the Seoseokdae and Ipseokdae columnar cliffs, natural stone pillars protected as a national monument. The Uijae art museum sits on its lower slopes.
tips: The Jeungsimsa temple entrance is the easiest starting point from the city.
Wear proper shoes — the upper trails are rocky.
Autumn foliage and spring azaleas are the peak seasons.
Start from the Jeungsimsa temple gate for the easiest route up; wear grippy shoes for the rocky upper trails, and time it for spring azaleas or autumn colour.

gwangju-museum.name: Gwangju National Museum
gwangju-museum.blurb: A calm, free museum of Jeolla-region history and art, famous for relics raised from a medieval shipwreck.
intro: The Gwangju National Museum gathers the art and history of the Jeolla region inside a graceful traditional-style building at the foot of the hills.
Its best-known collection is the haul of ceramics and cargo recovered from the Sinan shipwreck off Korea's southwest coast.
tips: General admission is free.
Allow a couple of hours, then pair it with a walk on nearby Mudeungsan.
It sits a little outside the centre — easiest by taxi or bus.

hahoe-village.name: Hahoe Folk Village
hahoe-village.blurb: A UNESCO-listed clan village of tiled and thatched houses cradled in a bend of the Nakdong River.
intro: Hahoe is a centuries-old village near Andong where people still live among the tiled mansions and thatched cottages of an old Confucian clan.
The Nakdong River loops right around it — the name means 'river-surrounding' — and it is a UNESCO World Heritage site.

The Ryu clan's village dates back some 600 years and keeps a layout arranged by pungsu (Korean geomancy) within the river's bend. UNESCO listed it in 2010 alongside Yangdong, and the Byeongsan Seowon Confucian academy stands nearby.
tips: Climb to the Buyongdae cliff across the river for the classic view over the whole village.
Check the schedule for the Hahoe mask dance, a lively local folk performance.
It's a bus or taxi ride from Andong; pair it with the mask museum at the entrance.
The Hahoe Byeolsingut mask dance runs on a set schedule — check the times. A shuttle bus links it to Andong, and the Andong Mask Museum sits at the village entrance.

byeongsan-seowon.name: Byeongsan Seowon
byeongsan-seowon.blurb: A serene UNESCO Confucian academy famous for the river view framed by its open Mandaeru pavilion.
intro: Byeongsan Seowon is a beautifully sited Confucian academy near Andong, among the Korean seowon inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage site.
Its open Mandaeru pavilion frames a much-loved view of the river and the cliff face opposite.

Moved to this riverside setting in 1613 and honouring the statesman Ryu Seong-ryong, Byeongsan Seowon is one of nine Korean seowon jointly inscribed by UNESCO in 2019. Its open Mandaeru pavilion is celebrated for framing the Nakdong River and the Byeongsan cliff opposite.
tips: Sit on the Mandaeru pavilion floor and take in the framed river view — the highlight of a visit.
It's quiet and uncrowded; combine it with Hahoe Village nearby.
Access is by car or taxi from Andong along a country road.
Sit on the Mandaeru pavilion floor for the framed river view — the highlight of a visit; it's quiet and uncrowded, reached by car or taxi from Andong, and pairs with Hahoe Village nearby.

odongdo.name: Odongdo
odongdo.blurb: A little island of camellia woods and sea-walk paths, linked to Yeosu by a breakwater.
intro: Odongdo is a small, forested island just off Yeosu, joined to the mainland by a long breakwater you can walk or ride a little dongbaek train across.
In late winter its camellia trees bloom red, and shaded paths lead to a lighthouse and sea-view lookouts.

The island is cloaked in thousands of camellia trees and dense bamboo, and legend ties its name to a phoenix said to have fed on its paulownia (odong) trees. A lighthouse at its tip helps guide ships into Yeosu.
tips: Walk the breakwater out, or hop on the trolley-style dongbaek train.
Camellias flower from late winter into early spring.
Pair it with the Yeosu waterfront and cable car nearby.
Walk the roughly 700 m breakwater out to the island or ride the little dongbaek train; camellias peak from late winter into spring, and it pairs with the Yeosu cable car and night-lit waterfront.

dolsan-bridge.name: Dolsan Bridge
dolsan-bridge.blurb: The illuminated bridge to Dolsan Island — the glowing heart of Yeosu's famous night sea.
intro: Dolsan Bridge arcs across the water to Dolsan Island, lit up in shifting colours after dark — the image most people picture as Yeosu's night sea.
The waterfront promenade and cafes below make it a favourite evening stroll.
tips: Come after sunset for the illuminated bridge and its reflection on the water.
Walk up to Dolsan Park for the classic overlook.
Seafood restaurants line the shore on the Dolsan side.

hyangiram.name: Hyangiram Hermitage
hyangiram.blurb: A tiny hermitage clinging to sea cliffs at the tip of Dolsan Island, famous for sunrise.
intro: Hyangiram is a small hermitage built into the rocky cliffs at the southern tip of Dolsan Island, reached by a steep path and narrow rock passages.
It looks straight out over the open sea and is one of Korea's celebrated spots to watch the sunrise.

Founded in 644 in the Silla era, Hyangiram is one of Korea's four celebrated seaside prayer sites. Pilgrims squeeze through narrow rock clefts to reach halls perched over the water, and its New Year sunrise festival draws big crowds.
tips: Wear good shoes — the final climb squeezes through narrow rock clefts.
Sunrise is the signature experience, so go early.
It's at the far end of Dolsan Island, best reached by car or bus.
Wear good shoes for the steep steps and rock passages, go at dawn for the signature sunrise, and it's at the far tip of Dolsan Island — best reached by car or bus from Yeosu.

dongpirang.name: Dongpirang Village
dongpirang.blurb: A hillside warren of alleys painted with murals, looking down over Tongyeong's old harbor.
intro: Dongpirang is a steep old neighbourhood above Tongyeong's Gangguan harbor, saved from demolition and covered in bright murals by artists and volunteers.
Climbing its painted lanes rewards you with harbour views and photo-perfect corners at every turn.

The name means 'east cliff'. When the hillside neighbourhood was slated for demolition around 2007, a public mural competition instead turned its walls into an open-air gallery — earning it the nickname Tongyeong's Montmartre — and the murals are repainted periodically to keep them fresh.
tips: Wear comfortable shoes — the lanes are steep and stepped.
The murals change over time as new ones are painted, and people still live here, so be respectful.
Combine it with Jungang Market at the bottom of the hill.
Climb the stepped lanes for harbour views, but keep your voice down — people still live here — and combine it with the lively Jungang Market and Gangguan waterfront below.

tongyeong-cablecar.name: Tongyeong Cable Car
tongyeong-cablecar.blurb: A long cable car up Mireuksan for a sweeping view over the Hallyeo maritime park's islands.
intro: The Tongyeong Cable Car climbs Mireuksan mountain, one of the longest such rides in the country, gliding over forest to a ridge-top station.
From the top, walkways lead to lookouts over the scattered islands of the Hallyeo Waterway.

The Hallyeosudo Viewing cable car runs about 1,975 m up Mireuksan, among the longest in Korea. From the ridge you look out over the islands of the Hallyeo Waterway, and on the clearest days as far as Japan's Tsushima; a luge track and a temple sit near the base.
tips: Buy tickets early and expect a queue on busy weekends.
Short trails at the top lead to the best island viewpoints.
Clear days give the widest sea views.
Buy tickets early and expect queues on busy weekends; short ridge trails lead to the best island viewpoints, and it pairs with the Dongpirang mural village and Jungang Market below.

hansando.name: Hansando
hansando.rank: Island of the great sea battle
hansando.blurb: A peaceful wooded island off Tongyeong, site of Admiral Yi's famous Hansan naval victory.
intro: Hansando is a quiet, green island a short ferry from Tongyeong, ringed by calm waters and pine-covered shores.
It is remembered as the site of Admiral Yi Sun-sin's celebrated Hansan Island victory, marked today by the Jeseungdang shrine.

In 1592 the island's waters saw Admiral Yi Sun-sin crush a Japanese fleet at the Battle of Hansan Island, using his famous 'crane wing' formation — one of the turning points of the Imjin War. The Jeseungdang shrine and its lookout pavilion honour him today.
tips: Take the ferry from Tongyeong's passenger terminal.
Visit the Jeseungdang shrine and its sea-view pavilion.
It makes an easy, restful half-day trip.
Take the ferry from Tongyeong's passenger terminal, visit the Jeseungdang shrine and its sea-view pavilion, and enjoy the quiet pine shores on an easy, restful half-day.
